## Study Design

FWI1987 and FWI2025 differ in version and in input resolution simultaneously, so comparing one against the other answers no question about either. Three series were computed from a single hourly weather record, and each contrast moved one thing (@tbl-design).

| Series | System  | Weather input               | Pathway                        |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| S1     | FWI1987 | daily 13:00 LDT observation | the legacy configuration       |
| S2     | FWI2025 | daily 13:00 LDT observation | pathway C of @cffdg2025fwi2025 |
| S3     | FWI2025 | observed hourly weather     | pathway A of @cffdg2025fwi2025 |

: The three fire danger series and what separates them. {#tbl-design}

S1 against S2 isolated the version change at fixed input, S2 against S3 isolated the input resolution change at fixed version, and S1 against S3 was the operational contrast an agency faces on migration, the sum of the other two. All three ran on the same weather, the same season window, the same startup values and the same gap filling, so nothing that differed between them was an artefact of the record.

Pathway C is the report's own procedure for the legacy observation. The 13:00 observation was converted to estimated daily maxima and minima using national constants, daily maximum temperature being about 2 degrees Celsius above the 13:00 value, minimum wind speed 10 per cent of it and maximum wind speed 30 per cent above it, and humidity carried through at constant vapour content; those maxima and minima were then expanded to an hourly stream by the sinusoidal method of @beck1989diurnal with the default offset and decay coefficients of Table A-1 of @cffdg2025fwi2025. Daily rainfall, whose timing is unknown in a once-daily observation, was placed at the first hour after sunrise, which is the rule the report gives and the rule FWI1987 implicitly used.

The literature behind the expectations set out in the Introduction was gathered under a written protocol on 13 October 2026, with search terms drawn from the title and keywords, run on the author's reference store, OpenAlex, NASA ADS and Semantic Scholar, and followed by one round of citation chasing through OpenAlex from six central papers. The searches (@fig-review-flow) retrieved `r n_fmt(review_counts$Records[1])` records, `r n_fmt(review_counts$Records[2])` of them unique, of which `r n_fmt(review_counts$Records[3])` were excluded on title and abstract, `r review_counts$Records[5]` were retained and `r review_counts$Records[4]` were read in full. One reader screened and read, Semantic Scholar refused one of the four queries, and NASA ADS ran the trend query without its trend concept because that word is a stopword there, so that strand is under-searched for the first question.

## Index Computation

FWI2025 was computed with the reference implementation published by the Canadian Forest Service Fire Danger Group [@nrcan2026cffdrsng], run unmodified at the version cited. It reproduced the standard output distributed with it exactly, to the last decimal place the file carries, over the 2,623 hour Petawawa Research Forest test record.

FWI1987 was implemented for this study in Python, so that both systems ran inside one process on one record, and the implementation was checked in two ways, both reported in the results. The first check was against the CRAN package `cffdrs`, version 1.9.2 [@wang2017cffdrs; @wang2026cffdrspkg], an independently published implementation maintained by the Canadian Forest Service, run through R over the same test record. The second was against the FWI1987 codes that BC Wildfire Service itself computed operationally at these stations at the time, which the data mart preserves alongside the raw observations, so that a different party, different code and a different decade met the same weather.

Two constants differ between @vanwagner1987fwi as printed and @vanwagner1985fortran as programmed, and this implementation followed the program. The moisture transform coefficient is 147.2772, not the rounded 147.2 of the report, since 59.5 x 250 / 101 = 147.27722772 is the value that closes the scale; and the Duff Moisture Code moisture functions take the listing's form. Using the rounded constants instead moved the Fine Fuel Moisture Code by up to 3.9 units over the test record, which would have entered a version comparison as a difference between systems when it is a difference between roundings.

## Seasonal Metrics

Six seasonal metrics were computed per station, season and series over the 1 May to 30 September window, namely mean Fire Weather Index, seasonal severity rating as the sum of the Daily Severity Rating, peak Buildup Index, and counts of days above each of the thresholds described next. Because FWI2025 produces an hourly value and FWI1987 a daily one, the FWI2025 series were summarised to a daily value at 16:00 Local Standard Time, which is 17:00 local daylight time. That hour is the conventional peak burn hour, and it is the modal hour of peak burning conditions in the reference implementation's own distributed output. It was not chosen from this record; for comparison, the modal hour of daily maximum summer temperature here was `r tz$modal_hour_of_max_temp_summer`:00 Local Standard Time. The daily maximum over all 24 hours was carried as a sensitivity and not as the primary, because the maximum of 24 draws exceeds a single daily value for reasons that have nothing to do with the version change.

The second question turns on the thresholding, so both schemes were built and neither was preferred.

Absolute thresholds are fixed numbers on the index scale applied unchanged to all three series, which is the scheme an agency uses, because a danger class is a number in a manual. @taylor2006science traced how Canadian danger classes were set from correlations between Fire Weather Index System values and historical fire occurrence, and reported that British Columbia defined its classes from the Fire Weather Index and the Buildup Index separately for three danger regions with different fire climates. Three thresholds were used. FFMC 91 was taken from section 4.1 of @cffdg2025fwi2025, so that counting days above it tested that report's comparability sentence directly, and it is also the value above which the Canadian Wildland Fire Information System classes the Fine Fuel Moisture Code as extreme [@field2015gfwed]. A Fire Weather Index above 30 is that system's extreme class [@field2015gfwed], and a Fire Weather Index above 19 is the fire spread day threshold of @podur2011spread, which @mcelhinny2020era5 used to count spread days in their global reanalysis. @field2015gfwed noted that such extreme thresholds "will be different in other regions" [@field2015gfwed, p. 1409], so the absolute counts here are Canadian classes applied to one basin and not local calibrations.

Relative thresholds are percentiles of each series' own distribution over a common reference period, taken as 1991 to 2020, the current World Meteorological Organization normal, and fixed before any metric was computed. Climate extremes monitoring moved to thresholds of this kind because, in the review of @zhang2011indices, "few physically based thresholds have relevance in all parts of the world" [@zhang2011indices], and @jain2017seasonlength used the 99th percentile of the Fire Weather Index alongside counts of spread days for North America. British Columbia uses a threshold of the same kind operationally, since the head fire intensity layer of the provincial strategic threat analysis "was developed using the 90th percentile fire weather index value for an interpolated and elevation-adjusted analysis of weather station values" [@bcws2026psta]. A day above a series' own 90th percentile means the same thing in each series by construction, so a difference in trend under relative thresholds cannot be an artefact of the two systems sitting at different levels.

Percentile counts carry two known problems. @zhang2005percentile showed by Monte Carlo simulation that sampling error in a threshold estimated from a fixed base period leads to "overestimated exceedance rates outside the base period" [@zhang2005percentile, p. 1641] and underestimated rates inside it, producing an artificial jump at the boundary, larger for higher percentiles and for positively autocorrelated observations, that a linear trend fitted across it reads as a trend, and they removed it with a bootstrap estimate of the in-base rates. That correction was applied here. For each season inside the 1991 to 2020 base period, the threshold was re-estimated with that season removed and each other base season in turn duplicated in its place, and the count for the season was the mean over those replacements, while the last `r yr_last - 2020` seasons, which lie outside the base period, used the threshold from the whole base period. @zhang2005percentile estimated a threshold for each calendar day, whereas the threshold here was estimated from all days of the season pooled, so the procedure was adapted from a daily to a seasonal threshold. @dunn2022reference then showed that trends computed from the same data over the same years differ when the reference period changes and the climate has shifted between the two periods, by about 1 day per decade, around 25 per cent, in the global HadEX3 warm-day index over 1961 to 2018 and by about 3 days per decade, around 50 per cent, at De Bilt [@dunn2022reference, p. 8]. That problem has no correction, because it is a property of the choice rather than an error in the estimate, so the reference period was fixed before any metric was computed and a relative-threshold trend here is a statement about the 1991 to 2020 period as well as about its index.

One property of that construction is stated because it resembles a result and is not one. Inside the reference period the mean number of days above a series' own 90th percentile is close to ten per cent of the days in it, in every series, by construction. The level of a relative count therefore carries no information about the version at all, and only its trend does.

Reference distributions were computed per station as well as per series, because pooling them would mix a valley station at `r round(min(stn_tbl$ELEVATION))` m with a ridge station at `r n_fmt(round(max(stn_tbl$ELEVATION)))` m, and the percentile would then describe the network rather than the site.

## Statistical Analysis

Trends were estimated with the non-parametric pairing that fire weather trend studies have adopted, the Theil-Sen slope with a Mann-Kendall test. @jain2017seasonlength applied that pairing to the potential fire season length and to the 99th percentile of the Fire Weather Index across North America from 1979 to 2015, computing the System from the North American Regional Reanalysis with field significance testing and a Canadian series truncated because the reanalysis ceased to assimilate Canadian precipitation observations after 2002, and @venalainen2014europe applied it to the Fire Weather Index over Europe from 1960 to 2012 with a Mann-Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation through an effective sample size, computing trends separately for the ERA-40 and ERA-Interim reanalyses. The Theil-Sen slope, the median of all pairwise slopes [@sen1968slope], was computed here over the `r n_seasons` seasons from `r yr_first` to `r yr_last` that survived the coverage rule, on the actual season numbers so that a gap in the sequence was honoured rather than treated as a step of one. The median of pairwise slopes was preferred to least squares because @hirsch1982trend showed that it was an unbiased estimator of a linear trend with considerably higher precision than a regression slope on highly skewed data, and seasonal counts of extreme days are skewed.

Significance was the Mann-Kendall test [@mann1945nonparametric] with the variance correction of @hamed1998mmk, which inflates the variance of the test statistic by the serial correlation present in the series rather than assuming independence. Serial correlation alters the variance of the Mann-Kendall statistic [@yue2002autocorrelation] and gives too large a rejection rate on trendless series [@bayazit2007prewhiten], and the literature offers four responses, prewhitening, trend-free prewhitening, variance correction and block bootstrap resampling [@onoz2012blockbootstrap]. Prewhitening was not used. @bayazit2007prewhiten found by simulation that it corrected the false rejection rate on trendless autocorrelated series but reduced the power of the test when a trend was present, and @yue2002autocorrelation showed that removing a positive serial correlation component by prewhitening also reduced the magnitude of the trend itself [see also @yue2002prewhitening]. The uncorrected result was reported alongside the corrected one only to show the size of the correction.

One approximation in that correction is stated here. Coverage dropped seasons out of the middle of some station records, so the season sequence was not evenly spaced. The Mann-Kendall statistic itself is unaffected, because it depends on the order of the values and not on their spacing, and the Theil-Sen slope was computed on the actual season numbers so a gap is a gap. The Hamed and Rao variance correction, however, estimates autocorrelation at lags counted in observations rather than in years, which across a gap compares seasons further apart than the lag says. The direction of that error is knowable, because it attributes to lag one a correlation measured over two or more years, which is smaller, so the correction applied was smaller than the true one and the test less conservative than it would be on a complete record. A marginal result is therefore weaker than its q value suggests.

Metric families were corrected within each series by the false discovery rate procedure of @benjamini1995fdr. The eight metrics in a family were computed from one series and rise and fall with the same fire weather, so their tests were not independent. @benjamini2001dependency proved that the same procedure still controls the false discovery rate when the test statistics have positive regression dependency on those of the true null hypotheses, which metrics driven by one weather record were expected to satisfy, and @wilks2016stippling showed by simulation that under moderate to strong correlation among tests the procedure becomes conservative rather than permissive. @wilks2016stippling also found that only 3 of the 281 papers published in the Journal of Climate in the first half of 2014, 1.1 per cent, considered multiple testing at all. Confidence intervals on a single slope were percentile intervals over 2,000 moving-block bootstrap resamples of seasons, with the block construction described next.

Comparing the trends of two records that share most of their variability has a precedent in the evaluation of atmospheric temperature data sets. @santer2000trenddiff tested the trend in the series of differences between two data sets rather than the overlap of their separate confidence intervals, because the difference removes variability common to both, and found that roughly 30 per cent of data set pairs differed significantly in lower tropospheric trend, mainly through differences in measurement system, where overlapping intervals had not shown it. @wilks1997resampling showed that applying the same resampling pattern to every element of a data vector carries the cross correlation between elements into the resampled statistics without the need to model it. The three series here came from one weather record and were strongly dependent, and each was also serially correlated from season to season. Resampling single seasons would keep the pairing between series but discard that serial correlation, which block bootstraps retain by resampling runs of consecutive observations [@kunsch1989bootstrap; @politis1994stationary], and @onoz2012blockbootstrap found that a block bootstrap Mann-Kendall test had power comparable with the other corrections for serial dependence. The difference between two series' slopes was therefore estimated by a moving-block bootstrap, drawing blocks of consecutive seasons with replacement and recomputing both slopes on the same resampled seasons in every one of 4,000 replicates, which kept the pairing between series by construction. Blocks were `r paste(sort(unique(vapply(as.integer(table(kept$station_name)[table(kept$station_name) >= 15]), block_length, integer(1)))), collapse = ' or ')` seasons long for station records of `r min(table(kept$station_name)[table(kept$station_name) >= 15])` to `r max(table(kept$station_name))` seasons, the cube root of the record length rounded up, which grows with the record but more slowly than it, as @kunsch1989bootstrap required for consistency, and they were drawn from the seasons in order of occurrence so that a gap in a station record fell inside a block. The interval on the difference was the plain percentile interval, on which the bias-corrected and accelerated interval of @efron1987better improves to second-order correctness [@diciccio1996bootstrap]. The two-sided p value was computed under the null hypothesis, following the first guideline of @hall1991guidelines, that resampling should reflect the null hypothesis, whose violation they found can seriously reduce power. The resampled differences were centred on the observed difference, and p was the share of them lying at least as far from it as the observed difference lies from zero. It was corrected for false discovery rate within the eight metrics of one contrast at one station.

Daily fire occurrence has been modelled statistically since Bruce (1960), whose negative binomial model related daily counts to a fire danger rating index and which @taylor2013prediction identified as the first stochastic model of fire occurrence. Canadian operational practice later moved to logistic models of fire presence, because, as @taylor2013prediction noted, "overdispersion is of concern when Poisson-based methods are used to model counts" [@taylor2013prediction, p. 591]. @martell1987logistic predicted the probability of a people-caused fire day in northern Ontario by logistic regression with a Poisson assumption for the daily count, and @martell1989seasonal added periodic functions of the calendar day to represent seasonal variation. Count models remain in use where the daily number is the quantity of interest. @plucinski2014bushfires modelled daily human-caused bushfires in south-west Western Australia by negative binomial regression on fuel moisture, fitted on three years and tested on an independent fourth, and @xiao2015count found that a negative binomial mixed model described forest fire counts in Guizhou, China, better than Poisson, zero-inflated and hurdle alternatives. The closest regional precedent is @magnussen2012bc, who modelled daily lightning- and human-caused fire occurrence across British Columbia from 1981 to 2000 by logistic regression on lightning strikes, forest cover, surface weather, atmospheric stability and Fire Weather Index System moisture codes, and under leave-one-year-out cross-validation predicted the daily provincial number of lightning fires at R = 0.83 and of human-caused fires at R = 0.55 [@magnussen2012bc]. @granville2022case supplied the one Canadian test of whether the relationship between danger and occurrence changed over time, fitting period by intensity interactions to industrial fires in Ontario from 1976 to 2019 and finding "insufficient evidence to justify the inclusion of interaction terms for low HFI (p-value > 0.3, Table 3)".

Daily ignition counts here were modelled by negative binomial regression with a log link [@lawless1987negbin], because the response was a daily basin count rather than a cell-day presence. The linear predictor carried the daily basin danger value, two annual harmonics in day of year in the manner of @martell1989seasonal, season as a factor, and the number of stations that contributed to the basin mean that day, since no station reports in every season and the composition of the network changes. That last term cannot affect the comparison between series in any case, because all three are averaged over exactly the same stations on exactly the same days. The seasonal terms matter beyond this study, since @castelclavera2025comparative found in Mediterranean France that "relying solely on fire-weather indices is insufficient for efficient rating of fire activities" and that spatial and seasonal effects were needed, even though the Canadian Fire Weather Index was the most skilful index they tested. The lightning model carried no strike term, because no strike record covered the window, and lightning occurrence models depend on one. @flannigan1991lightning explained nearly 50 per cent of the variance in daily lightning fire counts in northwestern Ontario with the Duff Moisture Code and the multiplicity of negative discharges, @wotton2005lightning found that a sheltered duff moisture index was the strongest predictor of ignition given a strike, and @wierzchowski2002lightning recorded one fire for every 50 lightning discharges in British Columbia against one for every 1,400 in Alberta. The Canadian Lightning Detection Network climatology of @kochtubajda2020cldn covers 1999 to 2018, so it misses the first `r 1999 - yr_first` seasons of this window and the last `r yr_last - 2018`.

Predictive skill was compared by leaving one season out at a time, refitting without it, and scoring the held-out season, which is the blocked cross-validation @roberts2017crossvalidation recommend for temporally structured data, since random splits of such data result "in serious underestimation of predictive error" [@roberts2017crossvalidation], and the leave-one-year-out design @magnussen2012bc used for British Columbia. Each held-out season was scored by its log likelihood under the refitted model, the logarithmic score that @gneiting2007scoring showed to be strictly proper. They also noted that scores for competing forecasts "are directly comparable if they refer to exactly the same set of forecast situations" [@gneiting2007scoring, p. 362], which held here because the three series were scored on the same days. Series were compared on held-out likelihood rather than on in-sample fit because three series computed from one weather record will all fit, and the question is which predicts. One caution from the index comparison literature applies directly. @eastaugh2012cautionary compared four hypothetical indices, three of them simple transformations of one another, and found that all the established comparators they examined except the c-index "indicate different predictive power between the effectively identical indices", the differences "resulting from the frequency distributions of the index values rather than from any real difference in predictive power" [@eastaugh2012cautionary, p. 932]. The three series here are close to transformations of one another, and a log-linear danger term is sensitive to the shape of their distributions, so a small likelihood difference between them is not evidence of a difference in predictive power.

What a window of `r n_seasons` seasons cannot resolve was computed rather than hedged, following @weatherhead1998detection, who showed that the number of years needed to detect a trend grows with the variance and the lag-one autocorrelation of the noise, from about 10 to more than 20 years for a trend of 5 per cent per decade, and that a level shift from a change of instrument or site can raise that number by 50 per cent or more. @tiao1990autocorrelation had shown that the precision of a trend estimate depends critically on autocorrelation and on record length, and @wang2020power showed by simulation that the power of the Mann-Kendall test rises with slope and record length, falls with variance, and that positive autocorrelation increases both the Type I and the Type II error. For each metric the minimum detectable trend was the slope at which a two-sided test at alpha 0.05 would reach 80 per cent power given the residual spread of that metric about its own Theil-Sen line, adjusted for the lower efficiency of the Theil-Sen estimator under normal errors and inflated for serial correlation by the factor that @weatherhead1998detection derived for first-order autoregressive noise, the square root of (1 + phi) / (1 - phi), where phi is the lag-one autocorrelation of the residuals in season order. Phi was bounded between 0 and 0.9, so that a negative sample estimate could not make the detectable trend smaller than it would be for independent seasons. The extreme-day counts are counts of rare days, and @frei2001rare found that in a 100-year record a 1.5-fold change in the frequency of an event was detected with probability 0.6 when the event had an average return period of 30 days but only 0.2 at a return period of 100 days, so the least frequent thresholds were expected to be the least detectable. A null result was reported against the minimum detectable trend, so that "no trend detected" was kept separate from "no trend".


# Results {#sec-results}

```{r}
#| label: load-results
#| echo: true
#| output: false
series_daily <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "fwi-series-daily.csv"),
                         stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
series_daily$date <- as.Date(series_daily$date)
metrics <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "seasonal-metrics.csv"),
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
thresh_pct <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "threshold-percentiles.csv"),
                       stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
basin <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "basin-daily.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
basin$date <- as.Date(basin$date)

# Relative-threshold counts are replaced by the in-base bootstrap estimates of
# Zhang et al. (2005), computed from the same daily series and the same
# 1991 to 2020 base period. Out-of-base seasons are unchanged by construction;
# the check below stops the render if any is not.
corrected <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(SERIES), function(s)
  inbase_corrected_counts(series_daily, s, probs = c(90, 95),
                          reference = c(1991, 2020))))
for (pp in c(90, 95)) {
  col <- paste0("n_fwi_p", pp)
  cc <- corrected[corrected$prob == pp, c("station_name", "series", "year", "count")]
  key_m <- paste(metrics$station_name, metrics$series, metrics$year)
  key_c <- paste(cc$station_name, cc$series, cc$year)
  new <- cc$count[match(key_m, key_c)]
  out_base <- metrics$year > 2020 & is.finite(metrics[[col]])
  if (any(abs(new[out_base] - metrics[[col]][out_base]) > 1e-9))
    stop("in-base correction changed an out-of-base count for ", col)
  metrics[[paste0(col, "_uncorrected")]] <- metrics[[col]]
  metrics[[col]] <- new
}
```

## Implementation Checks

```{r}
#| label: tbl-verify
#| tbl-cap: "Verification of the FWI1987 implementation. The first block compares it against the CRAN package cffdrs over the Petawawa Research Forest test record. The second compares it against the FWI1987 codes BC Wildfire Service computed operationally at these stations, pooled over all kept station-seasons."
#| echo: true
val <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "fwi1987-validation.csv"),
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
opc <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "fwi1987-operational-check.csv"),
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# The two blocks differ by ten orders of magnitude, so the differences are
# formatted as strings rather than left to the table's numeric printing, which
# would render machine epsilon as a wall of zeros.
fmt_diff <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "", formatC(x, format = "g", digits = 3))

blk1 <- data.frame(
  Check = "against cffdrs",
  Component = val$component,
  n = format(val$n, big.mark = ","),
  `Max absolute difference` = fmt_diff(val$max_abs_diff),
  `Mean absolute difference` = fmt_diff(val$mean_abs_diff),
  `Correlation` = "",
  check.names = FALSE)

# The data mart names the operational columns in full; the initials are the
# component names used everywhere else in this document.
initials <- function(x) vapply(strsplit(x, "_"),
                               function(p) paste0(substr(p, 1, 1), collapse = ""),
                               character(1))
op_agg <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(opc, opc$component), function(d) {
  data.frame(
    Check = "against operational codes",
    Component = initials(d$component[1]),
    n = format(sum(d$n), big.mark = ","),
    `Max absolute difference` = "",
    `Mean absolute difference` = fmt_diff(weighted.mean(abs(d$mean_bias), d$n)),
    `Correlation` = formatC(weighted.mean(d$pearson_r, d$n), format = "f", digits = 4),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
rownames(op_agg) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(rbind(blk1, op_agg))
```

```{r}
#| label: verify-prose
#| echo: true
#| output: false
max_cffdrs <- max(val$max_abs_diff)
op_r <- weighted.mean(opc$pearson_r, opc$n)
op_n <- sum(opc$n)
bias_of <- function(comp) {
  d <- opc[opc$component == comp, ]
  weighted.mean(abs(d$mean_bias), d$n)
}
r_of <- function(comp) {
  d <- opc[opc$component == comp, ]
  weighted.mean(d$pearson_r, d$n)
}
dc_bias <- bias_of("DROUGHT_CODE")
bui_bias <- bias_of("BUILDUP_INDEX")
ffmc_r <- r_of("FINE_FUEL_MOISTURE_CODE")
```

@tbl-verify gives both checks. Against `cffdrs` the two implementations agreed to `r formatC(max_cffdrs, format = "g", digits = 2)` across all seven components, which is machine precision, because they are the same arithmetic, and the check confirmed that the equations were transcribed correctly rather than that they are correct.

Against the operational codes, computed by a different party in a different decade, the weighted mean correlation over `r n_fmt(op_n)` station-days was `r round(op_r, 3)`. That check was not expected to be exact, and one of its disagreements was large and had a known cause. The mean absolute bias in the Drought Code was `r round(dc_bias, 0)` units, and in the Buildup Index, which is computed from it, `r round(bui_bias, 1)`. BC Wildfire Service overwinters the Drought Code, carrying it from the previous autumn, whereas this study restarted it at 15 on 1 April, because these stations report no winter weather for an overwintering calculation to use. That is a difference in convention, not an error, and its direction is known, in that a restarted Drought Code is lower than an overwintered one. Every absolute Drought Code and Buildup Index level reported here is conditional on that convention, and it cannot affect any comparison between the three series, because all three restart identically.

The components that do not depend on the overwintered code agreed closely. The Fine Fuel Moisture Code correlated `r round(opc$pearson_r[opc$component == "FINE_FUEL_MOISTURE_CODE"] |> weighted.mean(opc$n[opc$component == "FINE_FUEL_MOISTURE_CODE"]), 4)` with the operational value, which is the component the version comparison principally rests on.

## Threshold Positions

```{r}
#| label: tbl-thresholds
#| tbl-cap: "Where each absolute threshold falls in each series' own 1991 to 2020 reference distribution, averaged over stations. A threshold at the same percentile in every series would mean the three systems are interchangeable for counting extremes. The reference median is the median of that component over the same distribution."
#| echo: true
tp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(thresh_pct, list(thresh_pct$series, thresh_pct$component,
                         thresh_pct$threshold), drop = TRUE),
  function(d) data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    Component = toupper(d$component[1]),
    Threshold = d$threshold[1],
    `Percentile of threshold` = round(mean(d$percentile_of_threshold, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    `Days per season above` = NA_real_,
    `Reference median` = round(mean(d$reference_median, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    check.names = FALSE)))
# Days per season above each absolute threshold, averaged over station-seasons.
days_above <- function(series, component, thr) {
  col <- switch(paste(component, thr),
                "ffmc 91" = "n_ffmc_ge91",
                "fwi 19" = "n_fwi_ge19",
                "fwi 30" = "n_fwi_ge30")
  mean(metrics[[col]][metrics$series == series], na.rm = TRUE)
}
key <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(rownames(tp), "\\."))
tp$`Days per season above` <- round(mapply(days_above, key[, 1], key[, 2],
                                           as.numeric(key[, 3])), 1)
tp <- tp[order(tp$Component, tp$Threshold, tp$Series), ]
rownames(tp) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(tp)
```

```{r}
#| label: threshold-prose
#| echo: true
#| output: false
ffmc91 <- subset(tp, Component == "FFMC" & Threshold == 91)
fwi19 <- subset(tp, Component == "FWI" & Threshold == 19)
p_s1 <- ffmc91$`Percentile of threshold`[grepl("S1", ffmc91$Series)]
p_s2 <- ffmc91$`Percentile of threshold`[grepl("S2", ffmc91$Series)]
p_s3 <- ffmc91$`Percentile of threshold`[grepl("S3", ffmc91$Series)]
d_s1 <- ffmc91$`Days per season above`[grepl("S1", ffmc91$Series)]
d_s2 <- ffmc91$`Days per season above`[grepl("S2", ffmc91$Series)]
d_s3 <- ffmc91$`Days per season above`[grepl("S3", ffmc91$Series)]
```

@tbl-thresholds tests the comparability sentence of @cffdg2025fwi2025 directly. A Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91 sat at the `r p_s1`th percentile of the S1 distribution, the `r p_s2`th of S2 and the `r p_s3`th of S3, which in days per season above it was `r d_s1` under S1, `r d_s2` under S2 and `r d_s3` under S3.

```{r}
#| label: threshold-reading
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The comparability claim is about where a value sits, so the reading is stated
# in the two units that matter and neither is rounded away: the percentile spread
# across series, and the difference in days per season an agency would count.
pct_spread <- max(abs(p_s3 - p_s1), abs(p_s2 - p_s1))
day_gap <- d_s3 - d_s1
day_gap_pct <- 100 * day_gap / d_s1
```

The claim survived as a statement about levels and did not survive as a statement about counts. The three medians of the Fine Fuel Moisture Code over the reference period sat within about a unit of each other, so a value of 91 does mean much what it used to mean, but the same threshold selected `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(day_gap))` `r if (day_gap >= 0) "more" else "fewer"` days per season under S3 than under S1, a difference of `r sprintf("%.0f", abs(day_gap_pct))` per cent, because the percentile it occupied moved by `r sprintf("%.1f", pct_spread)` points. Those are the same distributions, described two ways, and @fig-distributions shows why, in that the curves sit almost on top of one another through the middle and separate where the threshold is.

```{r}
#| label: fig-distributions
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the daily Fine Fuel Moisture Code and the daily Fire Weather Index over all kept station-days under the three series, with the absolute thresholds marked. The comparability claim of the 2025 report concerns the position of a value on the scale; an extreme-day count concerns the mass beyond a threshold, which is a different quantity."
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1.4, 1), mgp = c(2.4, 0.7, 0), cex = 0.75)
cols <- c(s1 = "#1B4F72", s2 = "#B7950B", s3 = "#943126")

plot_dens <- function(cols_prefix, xlab, cuts, xlim) {
  dens <- lapply(names(cols), function(s) {
    v <- series_daily[[paste0(s, "_", cols_prefix)]]
    density(v[is.finite(v)], na.rm = TRUE)
  })
  ymax <- max(vapply(dens, function(d) max(d$y), numeric(1)))
  plot(NA, xlim = xlim, ylim = c(0, ymax * 1.05), xlab = xlab,
       ylab = "Density", main = "")
  for (i in seq_along(dens)) lines(dens[[i]], col = cols[i], lwd = 1.8)
  abline(v = cuts, lty = 3, col = "grey30")
  legend("topleft", legend = unname(SERIES), col = cols, lwd = 1.8, bty = "n",
         cex = 0.72)
}
plot_dens("ffmc", "Fine Fuel Moisture Code", 91, c(40, 101))
plot_dens("fwi", "Fire Weather Index", c(19, 30), c(0, 60))
par(op)
```

## Mechanism

```{r}
#| label: fig-mechanism
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Ten days of the hourly Fine Fuel Moisture Code at Penticton RS in August 2003, under FWI2025 driven by the observed hourly weather and under FWI2025 driven by the 13:00 observation alone. Both are the same system on the same days, and the only difference is the weather input the System received. The vertical lines mark 13:00 local daylight time, the hour FWI1987 observes, and 17:00, the hour a daily value conventionally represents."
ex <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "example-season-hourly.csv"),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
ex$t <- as.POSIXct(sprintf("%04d-%02d-%02d %02d:00:00", ex$yr, ex$mon, ex$day, ex$hr),
                   tz = "UTC")
win <- ex[ex$mon == 8 & ex$day >= 14 & ex$day <= 23, ]

op <- par(mar = c(3.2, 4, 1.2, 1), cex = 0.8)
plot(win$t, win$s3_ffmc, type = "l", col = cols["s3"], lwd = 1.6,
     ylim = range(c(win$s3_ffmc, win$s2_ffmc), na.rm = TRUE),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Fine Fuel Moisture Code", xaxt = "n")
lines(win$t, win$s2_ffmc, col = cols["s2"], lwd = 1.6)
axis.POSIXct(1, win$t, format = "%d %b")
# The hour markers are drawn thin and pale on purpose: they locate the two
# sampling hours without competing with the curves, which are the subject.
abline(v = win$t[win$hr == 12], col = "grey86", lty = 3, lwd = 0.6)
abline(v = win$t[win$hr == 16], col = "grey62", lty = 2, lwd = 0.6)
lines(win$t, win$s3_ffmc, col = cols["s3"], lwd = 1.6)
lines(win$t, win$s2_ffmc, col = cols["s2"], lwd = 1.6)
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.75,
       legend = c(unname(SERIES[c("s3", "s2")]),
                  "13:00 LDT, the FWI1987 observation", "17:00 LDT"),
       col = c(cols["s3"], cols["s2"], "grey86", "grey62"),
       lwd = c(1.6, 1.6, 0.8, 0.8), lty = c(1, 1, 3, 2))
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-capability
#| tbl-cap: "Two quantities FWI2025 reports and FWI1987 cannot, the hour at which peak burning conditions occur and the number of hours per day the burning window stays open, both as the specification's own daily summary computes them. Values are means over kept station-seasons. FWI1987 has no entry because a system with one value per day cannot say when in the day it applies."
#| echo: true
cap <- metrics[metrics$series %in% c("s2", "s3") &
                 !is.na(metrics$mean_peak_hr), ]
if (nrow(cap)) {
  ct <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cap, cap$series), function(d) data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    `Mean peak hour (LST)` = round(mean(d$mean_peak_hr, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `Mean burning window (h)` = round(mean(d$mean_duration, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `Days per season with window >= 6 h` = round(mean(d$n_duration_ge6, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    check.names = FALSE)))
  rownames(ct) <- NULL
  fmt_tbl(ct)
} else {
  stop("seasonal-metrics.csv carries no daily summary columns; re-run build_seasonal_metrics.py")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: mechanism-reading
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The two readings the figure supports, computed from the same window it draws.
night <- win$hr %in% c(2, 3, 4, 5)
day <- win$hr %in% c(14, 15, 16, 17)
night_gap <- mean(win$s3_ffmc[night] - win$s2_ffmc[night], na.rm = TRUE)
day_gap <- mean(win$s3_ffmc[day] - win$s2_ffmc[day], na.rm = TRUE)
range_s3 <- mean(tapply(win$s3_ffmc, win$day, function(v) diff(range(v))))
range_s2 <- mean(tapply(win$s2_ffmc, win$day, function(v) diff(range(v))))
```

@fig-mechanism shows what separated S2 from S3 on the same ten days. Both are FWI2025, both were given the same rain, and the only difference was whether the System received the observed hourly weather or reconstructed a standard diurnal curve from the 13:00 observation.

The reconstruction was not a smoothed version of the observation but a different shape. Over these days it swung `r sprintf("%.1f", range_s2)` code units between its daily minimum and maximum against `r sprintf("%.1f", range_s3)` for the observed series, and the difference was concentrated overnight, in that the two ran `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(day_gap))` units apart in the mid-afternoon and `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(night_gap))` units apart before dawn. A standard curve anchored to one afternoon reading estimates the night, and it estimated it wetter than the nights actually were. @tbl-capability gives the consequence in the two quantities only the hourly system produces at all.

## Trends

```{r}
#| label: trend-compute
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The metric family. Each entry is a column of the seasonal metric table, a
# label, and which thresholding scheme it belongs to. The family is declared
# here, once, and the false discovery rate correction is applied within it.
METRICS <- data.frame(
  col = c("mean_fwi", "ssr", "peak_bui",
          "n_ffmc_ge91", "n_fwi_ge19", "n_fwi_ge30",
          "n_fwi_p90", "n_fwi_p95"),
  label = c("Mean FWI", "Seasonal severity rating", "Peak BUI",
            "Days FFMC >= 91", "Days FWI >= 19", "Days FWI >= 30",
            "Days above own 90th percentile", "Days above own 95th percentile"),
  scheme = c("level", "level", "level",
             "absolute", "absolute", "absolute",
             "relative", "relative"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Trends are estimated per station and per series, then combined, rather than on
# a basin average, because the set of reporting stations changes between seasons
# and a basin average would move when a station joins or leaves.
trend_rows <- list()
for (s in names(SERIES)) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(METRICS))) {
    m <- METRICS$col[i]
    for (stn in unique(metrics$station_name)) {
      d <- metrics[metrics$series == s & metrics$station_name == stn, ]
      d <- d[is.finite(d[[m]]), ]
      if (nrow(d) < 15) next
      tt <- trend_test(d$year, d[[m]])
      tt$series <- s; tt$metric <- m; tt$station <- stn
      tt$mdt <- minimum_detectable_trend(d$year, d[[m]])
      trend_rows[[length(trend_rows) + 1]] <- tt
    }
  }
}
trends <- do.call(rbind, trend_rows)
if (is.null(trends) || !nrow(trends))
  stop("No station has the 15 seasons the trend estimator requires. ",
       "Kept station-seasons: ", n_kept, " over ", n_seasons, " seasons. ",
       "Delete the weather record and the daily series and render again ",
       "to rebuild them over the full archive.")
# The family is the eight metrics within one series at one station.
trends$q <- ave(trends$p_corrected,
                paste(trends$series, trends$station), FUN = fdr)
write.csv(trends, file.path(outputs, "trend-estimates.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-trends
#| tbl-cap: "Theil-Sen slopes per season for each seasonal metric under each series, pooled across stations as the median station slope, with the range across stations. Significance is Mann-Kendall with the Hamed and Rao variance correction; the count is of stations at which the false discovery rate adjusted p value falls below 0.05 within that station's eight-metric family. The minimum detectable trend is the slope this record could resolve at 80 per cent power."
#| echo: true
tr <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(trends, list(trends$series, trends$metric),
                                  drop = TRUE), function(d) {
  data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    Metric = METRICS$label[match(d$metric[1], METRICS$col)],
    Stations = nrow(d),
    `Median slope` = round(median(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    `Slope range` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", min(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE),
                            max(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE)),
    `Stations q < 0.05` = sum(d$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Min detectable` = round(median(d$mdt, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
tr <- tr[order(match(tr$Metric, METRICS$label), tr$Series), ]
rownames(tr) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(tr)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-trends
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 7.0
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Seasonal metrics by season under the three series, pooled across stations as the station mean, with the Theil-Sen line for each series. The absolute and relative extreme-day counts are the panels the second question turned on, under the prediction that the absolute counts separate between series and the relative counts do not."
show <- c("mean_fwi", "ssr", "n_ffmc_ge91", "n_fwi_ge19", "n_fwi_p90", "n_fwi_p95")
# Generous bottom margin and tightened axis title placement: at three rows on one

op <- par(mfrow = c(3, 2), mar = c(3.8, 4, 1.4, 1), mgp = c(2.4, 0.7, 0),

for (m in show) {
  ylab <- METRICS$label[match(m, METRICS$col)]
  rng <- range(metrics[[m]], na.rm = TRUE)
  plot(NA, xlim = range(metrics$year), ylim = rng, xlab = "Season", ylab = ylab,
       main = "")
  for (s in names(SERIES)) {

    a <- aggregate(d[[m]], list(year = d$year), mean, na.rm = TRUE)
    points(a$year, a$x, col = cols[s], pch = 16, cex = 0.6)
    sl <- theil_sen(a$year, a$x)
    ic <- median(a$x - sl * a$year)
    abline(a = ic, b = sl, col = cols[s], lwd = 1.6)
  }
```
